newsitem.title: JAPAN: Matsushita set to put the focus on high-tech.
newsitem.headline: Matsushita set to put the focus on high-tech.

text.p: Japanese electronics behemoth Matsushita Electric plans to shift its focus from traditional consumer appliances to high-tech parts, aiming to transform its business and boost profits.

After struggling with razor-thin profits in the early 1990s, Matsushita Electric Industrial Co last week unveiled a new medium-term business strategy to transform itself and become more profitable, streamlined and sleeker.
Its products are sold under the National, Panasonic and Technics brand names.

Under a four-year "Development 2000" plan, Matsushita said it will focus on semiconductors and other key devices as well as the information sector, including optical discs, display devices and mobile phones.
It also announced a corporate restructuring which analysts said would make development of multimedia products much easier.

"We couldn't fully achieve our profitability target (a five percent return on sales) in the previous medium-term management plan," Matsushita public relations manager Susumu Ishihara told a news conference on Monday.
"But we plan to boost profitability under the new management strategy," he said.

Matsushita in the early 1990s suffered from saturation of the consumer electronics market and a lack of new hit products. But it has steadily raised sales and profits in the past three years on the strength of Japan's booming computer and information market.
It expects group net profit of 115 billion yen ($991 million) in the year to March 31, up seven percent when excluding foreign exchange losses from the 1995 sale of U.S. film maker MCA Inc.
Estimated 1996/97 group net profit would be 4.7 times that of 1993/94, when it was hurt by a consumer electronics slump.

Sales of profitable information and industrial machines such as mobile phones, CD-ROMs, hard disc drives and other computer peripherals, are expected to account for 32 percent of group sales in 1996/97, up from 25 percent three years ago.

But group net profits would be still under half the peak achieved in 1990/91. Analysts say its recovery is still slower than those of rivals Sony Corp and Sharp Corp, both of which have regained peak profit levels after shifts to lucrative high-tech parts and products business.
Under the new strategy, Matsushita said it would establish four internal division companies on April 1, grouping its 51 self-supporting business divisions.
The biggest group will converge its audiovisual and computer businesses for development of multimedia products.

"The restructuring will allow large and strategic investments in computer and information products by lowering stiff barriers between business divisions, which has hampered development of innovative products," said Katsuhiko Sugiyama, president of business consultant Musashi Business Development.
Matsushita also aims to boost parts and components production to 33 percent of the group's total output by March 2001, up from 28 percent in 1995/96.
It also plans to boost overseas production to 30 percent of the total and overseas sales and 50 percent by March 2001.
Analysts say, however, that the transformation at the giant company, boasting 7.4 trillion yen ($63.7 billion) in group sales, is still slow, due in part to its rigid corporate structure.
"Matsushita's strong ability in basic technology development has not been reflected in product development," said Sugiyama.
He said if adjustments are made to avoid duplication in such key areas as facsimiles and mobile phones, group operating profits could easily jump 20 percent. ($1=116 yen)
